chunks: "For an ideal inductor, impedance is j omega L.
At DC, omega is zero, so the impedance is zero: it's a short circuit, just a piece of wire, and a constant current produces no voltage.
As the frequency goes up, the impedance rises linearly, and as the frequency goes to infinity it goes to infinity, so it's an open circuit.

That matches the time-domain picture: v equals L di/dt, so to change the current quickly the inductor needs a huge voltage, which means it resists any very fast change, and at infinite frequency it behaves like an open.
On a log-log plot that's a straight line with a slope of plus 20 decibels per decade, passing through 2 pi times L ohms at 1 hertz. I'd add that this is the ideal behavior.

A real inductor has winding capacitance in parallel, so the curve rises up to the self-resonant frequency, peaks, and then falls like a capacitor, so at very high frequency it's effectively a capacitor, not an open circuit.

And since this is in the capacitor section, the capacitor is the mirror image: open circuit at DC and a short at infinite frequency, with impedance falling at minus 20 decibels per decade, until ESL turns it back up into an inductor."
